item.title: Pennsylvania's First Measles Deaths in 35 Years Spark a Bitter Vaccine Policy Clash Between Shapiro and RFK Jr.
item.body:
Pennsylvania has confirmed its first measles-related deaths in 35 years, a grim milestone that state officials say underscores how far childhood vaccination rates have slipped — and one that has quickly turned into a national political flashpoint.

## What Happened

State health officials confirmed that measles was a contributing factor in the deaths of several Pennsylvania residents this year, including an infant who had not been vaccinated against the disease. Pennsylvania's last measles fatality dated back to the late 1980s, before the widespread success of the two-dose MMR (measles, mumps, rubella) vaccination program drove the disease to the brink of elimination in the United States.

Public health experts note that measles is among the most contagious viruses known, capable of spreading through airborne droplets that can linger in a room for up to two hours after an infected person leaves. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) says two doses of the MMR vaccine are about 97 percent effective at preventing infection, and that community, or "herd," immunity generally requires around 95 percent of a population to be vaccinated to stop sustained outbreaks.

## A Public Disagreement Over the Cause

The deaths have opened a rift between Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro and U.S. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. Shapiro's administration has pointed to declining kindergarten vaccination rates in parts of the state — a trend mirrored nationally in recent years — as a key factor behind the outbreak, and has called for renewed public messaging in support of routine childhood immunizations.

Kennedy, who has long expressed skepticism about vaccine safety and oversight, has publicly questioned that framing, suggesting other factors may have contributed to the deaths and calling for a broader review of the state's health data before drawing conclusions. The exchange has played out largely through public statements and social media, with each side accusing the other of politicizing a public-health tragedy.

The disagreement reflects a wider national debate. Federal health agencies under Kennedy's leadership have faced scrutiny this year over changes to vaccine advisory panels and communication about immunization schedules, even as career public-health officials and major medical associations, including the American Academy of Pediatrics, continue to recommend the standard MMR schedule for children.

## Part of a Bigger National Trend

Pennsylvania's cases follow a difficult stretch for measles control nationwide. A large outbreak centered in West Texas in 2025 sickened hundreds of people and was linked to at least two deaths among unvaccinated children, marking some of the first U.S. measles fatalities in a decade. Health officials have since tracked smaller clusters in several other states, often tied to communities with lower-than-average vaccination coverage.

The CDC has cautioned that once measles is reintroduced into an under-vaccinated community, it can spread rapidly among people who are unvaccinated or whose immunity has waned, particularly infants too young to receive their first dose, which is typically given between 12 and 15 months of age.

## What Comes Next

Pennsylvania's Department of Health says it is continuing to investigate the source of the outbreak and is working with local hospitals to monitor for additional cases. Shapiro has asked state lawmakers to consider funding for expanded outreach to schools and pediatric clinics in under-vaccinated counties, while also pressing federal officials for clarity on national vaccine guidance.

Kennedy's office has indicated that federal health agencies will review the state's findings as part of a broader look at immunization data across the country. Both sides say they support parents having access to accurate information about vaccines, even as they diverge sharply on how the current situation should be characterized.

Medical groups, meanwhile, are urging families to check their children's vaccination records and consult a pediatrician or family physician with any questions about the MMR schedule, especially for infants, pregnant women, and people with weakened immune systems who face the highest risk from measles complications.
